---
title: "Analysis 1: How well do computational methods predict experimental ΔΔG?"
author: "Luis Sebastian Galán, Laura Grenaa Jensen, Taniya Dey and Thota Kanishka Rao"
format: html
---

## Setup

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("here")
library("broom")
```

## Load data

AB-Bind contains predictions from six computational methods. To compare
them fairly, we only keep mutations that have a prediction from all six
methods. That way, every method is tested on exactly the same mutations.

```{r}
dat_aug <- read_csv(here("data", "03_dat_aug.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

dat_complete <- dat_aug |>
  drop_na(ends_with("_ddg"))

dat_pred <- dat_complete |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with("_ddg"),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "predicted_ddg"
  ) |>
  mutate(method = str_remove(method, "_ddg"))

dat_pred |>
  count(method)
```

## Capped experimental values

Some mutations weaken binding so much that the change can no longer be
measured. In AB-Bind, these mutations are given a ΔΔG of exactly
8 kcal/mol, so a value of 8 really means "8 or more". Before comparing
the methods, we check how many of these capped values there are and
where they come from.

```{r}
dat_capped <- dat_complete |>
  filter(ddg >= 8)

dat_capped |>
  summarise(
    n_capped = n(),
    n_total = nrow(dat_complete),
    n_to_alanine = sum(to_alanine)
  )

dat_capped |>
  count(pdb, assay_name, sort = TRUE)
```

There are 26 capped values out of 542 mutations. Most of them come from
a single complex (1MHP) that was measured with ELISA.

## Predicted vs. experimental ΔΔG

Each point is one mutation. If a method predicted perfectly, all points
would fall on a straight line. The blue line is a linear fit, and the
row of points at 8 kcal/mol are the capped values.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
dat_pred |>
  ggplot(aes(x = predicted_ddg, y = ddg)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  facet_wrap(~ method, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    x = "Predicted ΔΔG",
    y = "Experimental ΔΔG (kcal/mol)",
    title = "Predicted vs. experimental ΔΔG for each computational method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Fitting one model per method

We fit a linear model, `ddg ~ predicted_ddg`, for each method using
`nest()` and `map()`. From each model we take the slope, its p-value and
the R squared, which tells us how much of the variation in experimental
ΔΔG the method explains.

We also calculate the Spearman correlation. Spearman does not look at
how close the predicted values are, only at whether the method puts the
mutations in the right order. That is useful in practice: when
improving an antibody, you mainly want to know which mutations to test
first.

To show how certain each correlation is, we add a 95% confidence
interval. We use the Fisher z-transformation with the variance
1.06 / (n - 3), which is the version recommended for Spearman
correlations (Fieller, Hartley and Pearson, 1957).

```{r}
models <- dat_pred |>
  group_by(method) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ lm(ddg ~ predicted_ddg, data = .x)),
    glance = map(model, glance),
    tidy = map(model, tidy),
    n = map_int(data, nrow),
    spearman = map_dbl(
      data,
      ~ cor(.x$ddg, .x$predicted_ddg, method = "spearman")
    )
  )

model_summary <- models |>
  unnest(glance) |>
  select(method, n, r_squared = r.squared, spearman) |>
  left_join(
    models |>
      unnest(tidy) |>
      filter(term == "predicted_ddg") |>
      select(method, slope = estimate, p_value = p.value),
    by = "method"
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    se_z = sqrt(1.06 / (n - 3)),
    spearman_low = tanh(atanh(spearman) - 1.96 * se_z),
    spearman_high = tanh(atanh(spearman) + 1.96 * se_z)
  ) |>
  select(-se_z) |>
  arrange(desc(spearman))

model_summary
```

## Comparing the methods

Each point is the Spearman correlation for one method, and the error
bars show the 95% confidence interval. The further to the right, the
better the method ranks the mutations.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
model_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = spearman, y = fct_reorder(method, spearman))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = spearman_low, xmax = spearman_high),
                 height = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(
    x = "Spearman correlation with experimental ΔΔG (95% CI)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "How well each method ranks the mutations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Conclusion

All six methods point in the right direction: mutations with a higher
predicted ΔΔG also tend to have a higher experimental ΔΔG, and every
slope is significant. Still, the predictions are weak. No method
explains more than 8% of the variation in experimental ΔΔG.

Discovery Studio (d_studio) is best at ranking the mutations
(Spearman 0.32), closely followed by FoldX (0.27). Their confidence
intervals overlap, so we cannot say that one is clearly better than
the other. Statium does worst, and its confidence interval almost
reaches zero.

One thing to keep in mind is the 26 capped values. Because they all
have the same value, they count as ties, and ties pull the Spearman
correlation slightly towards zero. This does not change our conclusions,
but the methods may rank the mutations a little better than these
numbers suggest.
